overview: This file documents the tightening and institutionalization of Japanese press censorship from January 1940 through October 1941. Embassy telegrams describe increasingly severe restrictions on foreign correspondents, press bans on sensitive political and diplomatic subjects, pressure to sell and consolidate newspapers, and the creation of a centralized Cabinet Intelligence Bureau. Later despatches and enclosures illustrate surveillance of the vernacular press and reproduce Imperial Ordinance No. 37, which prohibited publication of military and mobilization secrets and authorized suppression of reporting considered harmful to diplomacy or national policy. Cross-reference sheets broaden the subject to anti-Roosevelt commentary and cartoons and the Japanese prohibition on information bulletins issued by foreign missions.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Grew on censorship of foreign correspondents
subfiles.about: Reports a marked shift from censorship of Japan's domestic press toward drastic restriction of foreign correspondents' outgoing reports.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that the local press has become relatively less restrained while foreign correspondents' despatches are being heavily cut. Wilfrid Fleisher must submit his telephone reports to the New York Herald Tribune to a censor, who rejects even material already appearing in Japanese newspapers. Grew warns that American newspaper coverage from Tokyo will consequently provide an inadequate picture of Japanese affairs.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Telegram No. 723 on the Cabinet Intelligence Bureau
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a telegram concerning the projected Cabinet Intelligence Bureau and the scarcity of independent political writing.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references Telegram No. 723 in file 894.002/419. It notes indications that the projected Cabinet Intelligence Bureau would impose stricter censorship and records the recent scarcity of political articles and independent editorials in the vernacular press.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 723 on the projected Cabinet Intelligence Bureau
subfiles.about: Describes the organization of a centralized intelligence bureau and indications that it would intensify censorship of political and diplomatic reporting.
subfiles.summary: The proposed Cabinet Intelligence Bureau would absorb functions of the Army and Navy intelligence bureaus, the Foreign Office Information Bureau, the Home Office, and the Communications Ministry. It would also assume responsibility for press conferences formerly conducted by the Navy and Foreign Office. Reports circulating among journalists predicted stricter censorship resembling totalitarian publicity policy, while a ban covered reporting on negotiations with seven foreign powers; the Embassy had already observed a marked decline in political articles and independent editorial comment.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 853 on bans covering Cabinet and Axis negotiations
subfiles.about: Reports bans on speculation about extraordinary Cabinet meetings and on discussion of Japanese negotiations with the Axis powers.
subfiles.summary: A reliable American correspondent informed the Embassy that Japanese authorities had prohibited speculative comment on the subjects of extraordinary Cabinet meetings. A separate ban had recently forbidden press discussion of Japan's negotiations with the Axis powers.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 824 on censorship and newspaper consolidation
subfiles.about: Describes the effect of severe censorship on foreign correspondents and reported plans to force newspaper sales, mergers, and closures.
subfiles.summary: Grew states that both the Japanese press and outgoing foreign correspondence are so restricted that several foreign journalists hope to leave Tokyo. The Japan Times was pressuring Benjamin W. Fleisher to sell the Japan Advertiser, with its editor warning of increasing publication difficulties if no sale occurred. The projected information board was reportedly considering mergers of the Advertiser with the Times and of the Asahi with the Nichi Nichi, suppression of the latter's English edition, and consolidation of all afternoon newspapers.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 865 on Fleisher's censored reports and the proposed goodwill organization
subfiles.about: Explains two reports telephoned by Fleisher and assesses a proposed umbrella organization for Japanese international friendship societies.
subfiles.summary: Fleisher had telephoned the New York Herald Tribune about an extraordinary Cabinet meeting, a Hochi article advocating continued action in Indochina despite Anglo-American pressure, and a proposed cultural organization under Japan's “new structure.” Admiral Ogasawara and Yamamoto were selected to draft regulations for the organization, which would incorporate existing international societies. Grew did not know how much of Fleisher's reporting survived censorship and judged that the America-Japan Society could no longer promote genuine friendship; page 11 supplies a corrected version of the telegram's second page.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Eliot's report about Fleisher
subfiles.from: Department of State Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: Records George Fielding Eliot's report that Fleisher could no longer transmit anything beyond official communiqués.
subfiles.summary: Eliot telephoned from New York after the Herald Tribune received a message and call from Fleisher. Fleisher said censorship had made substantive reporting impossible and instructed the newspaper not to send him further funds after the end of the month. Tribune staff considered the message significant because Fleisher was regarded as particularly adept at circumventing censorship.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 356 requesting inquiry into Fleisher's call
subfiles.about: Asks the Embassy to consult Fleisher about the background to his telephone call to the New York Herald Tribune.
subfiles.summary: The Department suggests that the Embassy confer with Fleisher if he has not already approached it. The inquiry concerns the background of his September 17 telephone call to the New York Herald Tribune and is transmitted confidentially.

subfiles.title: Memorandum summarizing Despatch No. 5044
subfiles.about: Summarizes evidence that a newspaper faced punishment for publishing comments about the disappearance of European privileged classes.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes two translations enclosed with Tokyo's Despatch No. 5044. Authorities were reportedly angered by a Miyako column stating that privileged classes, especially the nobility, were disappearing during the European war. Officials regarded its possible implications for Japan's nobility as a dangerous thought, although the paper had not yet been suspended.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5044 on surveillance of the Miyako
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits two press translations illustrating official surveillance of potentially liberal ideas in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses a trade-paper report that the Tokyo daily Miyako risked suspension and the editorial passage believed to have caused the dispute. The passage argued that war was removing Europe's privileged governing classes, particularly the nobility. The Embassy believed the authorities feared readers might apply this observation to Japan and noted allegations that the Miyako retained the liberalism of an earlier era.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 1: Bulletin report on possible suspension of the Miyako
subfiles.about: Reports official anger over a Miyako article and the possibility that the newspaper would be suspended.
subfiles.summary: The translated trade-paper article says the authorities were increasingly irritated despite explanations from the Miyako's editorial staff. Officials believed ordinary journalistic judgment should have prevented publication of ideas contrary to national policy. A decision was expected within days, and some form of suspension was feared.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 2: Miyako excerpt on the disappearance of privileged classes
subfiles.about: Reproduces the passage asserting that Europe's privileged political classes were disappearing during the war.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt from the Miyako's “Political Sweepings” column argues that the European war was eliminating privileged groups, especially the nobility, which had controlled the old political order. It contrasts this continent-wide transformation with the previous World War, when such a transfer of power occurred only in Russia.

subfiles.title: Memorandum summarizing Despatch No. 5326
subfiles.about: Summarizes an Imperial ordinance restricting news publication and foreign correspondents' concerns about pending security legislation.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that Imperial Ordinance No. 37 prohibited publication of mobilization, military, and military-resource secrets and allowed the prime minister to suppress sensitive diplomatic or policy-related news. It also notes a pending National Defense Security Act intended to combat espionage. Foreign correspondents feared the new law's extraterritorial reach and possible effect on their reporting.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5326 on the Imperial press-control ordinance
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the Embassy's translation of Imperial Ordinance No. 37 and discusses its legal setting.
subfiles.summary: The despatch identifies the ordinance's prohibitions on mobilization and military secrets and its authorization of restrictions on diplomatic, financial, economic, and other policy-related reporting. Grew notes that the measure governed publications within Japan and rested on existing laws. He also reports the introduction of the broad and severe National Defense Security Act, whose possible application outside Japan alarmed foreign correspondents.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Translation of Imperial Ordinance No. 37
subfiles.about: Provides the translated ordinance authorizing censorship, prohibition, seizure, and penalties relating to sensitive publications.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance prohibits publication of designated mobilization secrets, military secrets, and military-resource information. It authorizes the prime minister to restrict news concerning diplomacy, information to be concealed from foreign countries, and matters thought likely to hinder financial, economic, or other national policies; offending publications and their originals may be seized. It extends administrative authority to Korea, Taiwan, southern Sakhalin, and the South Seas Mandate and appends extracts from the National General Mobilization Law specifying prison terms and fines for disclosure of secrets.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on criticism of Roosevelt's Far East statements
subfiles.about: Refers to an instruction enclosing disparaging Japanese-sponsored Chinese-language press commentary on Roosevelt's Far East remarks.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Instruction No. 2133 in the Roosevelt decimal file. That document enclosed a report of disparaging comment by the Sin Shun Pao, described as a Chinese-language newspaper organ of the Japanese Army, concerning President Roosevelt's press-conference statements on the Far East.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on an unfavorable Roosevelt cartoon
subfiles.about: Refers to a despatch containing an anti-Roosevelt cartoon and a conversation with editor Toshio Go.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references Despatch No. 5469 in the Roosevelt decimal file. The underlying despatch included copies of an unfavorable cartoon of President Roosevelt published in the Japan Times and Advertiser and a memorandum of conversation with its editor, Toshio Go.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on foreign missions' information bulletins
subfiles.about: Refers to a telegram reporting that foreign missions could no longer circulate information bulletins publicly in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to two-section Telegram No. 1594. It records a Japanese government decision barring foreign missions in Tokyo from publicly circulating information bulletins and other releases and notes a protest by British authorities.

interest: The file is especially useful for tracing how Japanese censorship evolved from selective interference with foreign reporting into a centralized and legally codified system. Its combination of confidential diplomatic reporting, journalists' personal reactions, merger plans, translated newspaper material, and the text of Imperial Ordinance No. 37 connects day-to-day censorship practices with broader institutional change. The corrected telegram page and numerous cross-references also expose the State Department's documentary workflow and point historians toward related files on Roosevelt, propaganda, and foreign missions.
